stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman who is up to date with her routine cervical screening. Her last cervical screening test five years ago was HPV not detected. She has had regular menstrual cycles, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, and is in a stable long term relationship.

Her routine cervical screening test today returns HPV oncogenic types other than 16 or 18 detected. A reflex liquid based cytology on the same sample shows low grade squamous intraepithelial lesion.

She is otherwise well, has never been immunised against HPV, and has no immunosuppression. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Prior screening: HPV not detected five years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy within eight weeks for direct visualisation and directed biopsy
options.rationale: Direct colposcopy is indicated for HPV 16/18 detected or non 16/18 with high grade cytology, symptomatic bleeding, or repeat HPV positive at 12 months; a single non 16/18 with LSIL does not meet referral criteria at first detection (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Return to routine five yearly HPV cervical screening as the reflex cytology is low grade
options.rationale: A five year interval applies only to HPV not detected results; any oncogenic HPV detection mandates earlier surveillance or colposcopy under the algorithm (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Prescribe topical imiquimod cream and repeat cytology alone in six months to assess clearance
options.rationale: Imiquimod is not a treatment for cervical HPV or LSIL and cytology alone has been superseded by primary HPV testing in Australia since December 2017 (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Arrange an HPV self collection swab in three months to confirm today's clinician collected result
options.rationale: Self collection is an alternative primary collection method now available to all screening eligible women, not a confirmatory test after a positive clinician collected result (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Repeat the HPV cervical screening test in 12 months to reassess persistence of the current infection
options.rationale: For HPV non 16/18 with any reflex cytology result of LSIL or lower and no prior high risk history, the NCSP directs a repeat HPV test at 12 months rather than immediate colposcopy, because most non 16/18 infections clear spontaneously (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

explanation.summary: The Australian NCSP moved to primary HPV screening in December 2017. Screening is five yearly from age 25 to 74 with self collection now available to all. The management pathway diverges by HPV type: HPV 16/18 detected refers directly to colposcopy regardless of cytology; HPV non 16/18 detected triggers reflex cytology, and low grade or negative cytology returns to a 12 month repeat HPV test rather than immediate colposcopy.
key_points: HPV 16/18 detected always refers directly to colposcopy.
HPV non 16/18 with negative or low grade cytology returns for repeat HPV at 12 months.
HPV non 16/18 with high grade cytology refers to colposcopy.
explanation.pearls: First detection of HPV non 16/18 with LSIL cytology returns at 12 months for repeat HPV, not straight to colposcopy - persistence at that second visit is what drives referral.

sources.label: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 38 year old woman six months after a large loop excision of the transformation zone for a histologically confirmed high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL, CIN 3). Excision margins were reported as clear of dysplasia and endocervical curettage was negative.

She has recovered well with no bleeding or unusual discharge. She has never smoked, is HIV negative, and is not on any immunosuppressive medication.

Her six month test of cure co test today returns HPV not detected and cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She asks when she should return for the next screen.

data_table.Procedure: LLETZ six months ago for CIN 3; margins clear; endocervical curettage negative
data_table.Test of cure today: HPV not detected; cytology NILM (co test)
data_table.Risk factors: Never smoker; HIV negative; not immunosuppressed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up?

options.text: Return to routine five yearly HPV cervical screening as she has cleared her treated lesion today
options.rationale: A single negative co test is insufficient because post treatment recurrence risk stays elevated for years; the protocol requires ongoing annual co tests until two consecutive negatives, not immediate return to five yearly (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Annual co test of HPV and cytology for the next 24 months and then return to routine screening
options.rationale: After treatment for HSIL the NCSP test of cure protocol requires an annual co test until two consecutive negative co tests are obtained, after which the woman returns to routine five yearly HPV screening (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Refer for repeat colposcopy in six months regardless of the negative test of cure result today
options.rationale: With clear margins, negative endocervical sampling, and a negative test of cure, repeat colposcopy is not indicated in the absence of an abnormal test result (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Arrange repeat cytology alone at 12 months without HPV testing given the treatment was successful
options.rationale: Cytology alone has lower sensitivity than co testing for post treatment recurrence and the NCSP mandates co testing (HPV plus cytology) during the test of cure period (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Offer completion hysterectomy after two children to remove any residual cervical cancer risk
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not indicated after successfully treated HSIL with negative surveillance and would be disproportionate; ongoing co test surveillance is the standard (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

explanation.summary: Test of cure surveillance after treatment for HSIL is one of the highest yield NCSP protocols. Recurrence risk after LLETZ remains elevated for at least a decade, and co testing catches persistent HPV that cytology alone misses. The requirement of two consecutive negative annual co tests before returning to routine five yearly screening is a defining Australian rule and a common exam discriminator against a return to routine screening after one negative test.
key_points: Post HSIL treatment requires annual co test (HPV plus cytology).
Two consecutive negative co tests are needed before return to five yearly screening.
A single negative test of cure does not end surveillance.
explanation.pearls: After LLETZ for CIN 2 or CIN 3, do annual HPV plus cytology co tests until two are consecutively negative, then resume five yearly HPV screening.

sources.label: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

stem:
You are the GP consulting a 22 year old woman who takes a combined monophasic 30 mcg ethinyloestradiol pill. She is in week two of her current pack. She forgot to take her pill on Wednesday and Thursday and realised this morning (Friday) when she opened the pack.

She has had unprotected sex on Tuesday evening. She has no other missed pills in this pack or the previous pack. She takes no other regular medications and has no contraindications to hormonal contraception.

She is otherwise well. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Missed pills: Two consecutive pills in week two of current pack

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Take the most recent missed pill and offer levonorgestrel emergency contraception because unprotected sex occurred
options.rationale: Emergency contraception is not required when pills are missed in week two provided the first seven days of the pack were completed correctly, because ovarian suppression has already been established (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Discard the current pack, start a new pack today, and use condoms for the next seven days for safety
options.rationale: Discarding the pack is not required and would prolong the pill free interval, increasing rather than decreasing the ovulation risk (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Take the two missed pills together now, skip the next pill free week, and start the next pack straight after
options.rationale: Only the most recent missed pill is taken; older missed pills are not doubled up. Skipping the pill free week is required only if missed pills fall in week three, not week two (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Take the most recent missed pill now, continue the pack, and use condoms for the next seven days
options.rationale: Two missed active pills in week two require taking the most recent missed pill immediately and using barrier cover for seven days; emergency contraception is not indicated because there were seven consecutive days of active pill taking before the missed pills (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Insert a copper intrauterine device within five days as emergency contraception given unprotected intercourse
options.rationale: A copper IUD is an option for emergency contraception up to five days after unprotected sex, but is not required here because established pill use before the missed pills provides ongoing suppression (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare, adopted by RACGP).

explanation.summary: Missed pill rules for combined oral contraception hinge on where in the pack the miss occurs. Week one misses risk ovulation because the pill free interval extends; week three misses risk ovulation because the coming pill free interval would prolong suppression loss. Week two misses with seven consecutive prior active pills usually maintain suppression, so barrier cover for seven days is sufficient without emergency contraception. Emergency contraception is only indicated for week one misses combined with unprotected sex during or shortly after the pill free interval.
key_points: Take the most recent missed pill immediately; do not double up older misses.
Two or more missed pills need seven days of barrier cover.
Emergency contraception is required only if misses occur in week one with recent unprotected sex.
explanation.pearls: Week two missed pills with prior seven days of consistent use need only seven days of condoms - no emergency contraception, no pack discard.

stem:
You are the after hours GP registrar consulting a 27 year old woman. She had a single episode of unprotected vaginal intercourse 72 hours ago and is worried about pregnancy. Her last menstrual period started 12 days ago and her cycles are regular at 28 days.

Her body mass index is 32 kg/m2. She takes no hormonal contraception and has never had an intrauterine device. She has no known drug allergies and no medical history of note. She specifically declines any device based contraception today for personal reasons and asks for a tablet option.

She is otherwise well and her vital signs are within normal limits. A urine pregnancy test today is negative.

data_table.Cycle position: Day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate emergency contraception?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg oral single dose taken as a one tablet regimen this evening
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is less effective than ulipristal at BMI over 26 and around ovulation; a doubled 3 mg dose is sometimes used but ulipristal is preferred when available (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg oral single dose taken as a one tablet regimen this evening
options.rationale: Ulipristal remains effective up to 120 hours after unprotected sex, and is more effective than levonorgestrel around the time of ovulation and in women with BMI over 26; she is near ovulation on day 12 of a 28 day cycle (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Levonorgestrel 3 mg oral single dose given her body mass index above 26 this evening
options.rationale: Doubling the levonorgestrel dose is an option in higher BMI but ulipristal is the preferred tablet given both raised BMI and mid cycle timing where ovulation is imminent (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Copper intrauterine device inserted within the next 48 hours by a trained clinician
options.rationale: Copper IUD is the single most effective emergency contraception but the patient has explicitly declined any intrauterine device today; her stated preference makes an oral option the correct choice (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Mifepristone 200 mg oral single dose taken as a one tablet regimen this evening
options.rationale: Mifepristone is not registered for emergency contraception in Australia and is licensed only for medical termination of pregnancy in combination with misoprostol (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Sexual and Reproductive Health).

explanation.summary: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception at any BMI or cycle position, but requires acceptance of a device. Among oral options, ulipristal outperforms levonorgestrel when ovulation is imminent (ulipristal delays ovulation even once the LH surge has begun, whereas levonorgestrel does not) and at BMI above 26. Ulipristal is effective up to 120 hours; levonorgestrel up to 96 hours. Ulipristal should be taken more than 5 days apart from any progestogen containing hormonal contraception because progestogen reduces its efficacy.
key_points: Ulipristal is preferred at BMI over 26 or when ovulation is imminent.
Ulipristal works up to 120 hours; levonorgestrel up to 96 hours.
Copper IUD is most effective if the patient accepts insertion.
explanation.pearls: Delay starting or restarting progestogen contraception for five days after ulipristal - progestogen blunts ulipristal efficacy.

stem:
You are the GP consulting a 24 year old woman who wants the most effective long acting reversible contraceptive available in Australia and who plans to try for pregnancy in about two years. She has heavy but regular menstrual periods that soak through a pad every hour on the first two days and cause her to miss work.

Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2, she has never been pregnant, and her blood pressure is within normal limits. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, migraine, or breast cancer. She takes no regular medications.

Her haemoglobin is 105 g/L (115-165) and ferritin is 8 mcg/L (20-200), consistent with iron deficiency anaemia.

data_table.Menstrual pattern: Regular; soaks pad hourly on day one and two
data_table.Reproductive plan: Wants pregnancy in about two years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line long acting reversible contraceptive?

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant lasting three years and inserted in the upper arm today
options.rationale: The implant is a highly effective LARC but commonly causes unpredictable bleeding rather than reducing menstrual loss, so is not the best choice when menorrhagia is the second problem to solve (Source: FSRH CEU Progestogen only implant).

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular injection every 12 weeks
options.rationale: DMPA reduces bleeding for some women but return to fertility can be delayed up to 12 months after cessation, which conflicts with her plan to conceive in two years (Source: FSRH CEU Progestogen only injectable).

options.text: 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device lasting up to eight years in Australia
options.rationale: The 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD is highly effective, treats heavy menstrual bleeding as a therapeutic indication, and reverses quickly on removal; it is a first line option here given both contraception and menorrhagia (Source: RANZCOG Heavy menstrual bleeding).

options.text: Copper intrauterine device lasting up to ten years and inserted within the next cycle
options.rationale: The copper IUD is effective contraception but typically increases menstrual blood loss, which would worsen her existing iron deficiency anaemia (Source: FSRH CEU Intrauterine contraception).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to skip withdrawal bleeds each month
options.rationale: The COCP is not a long acting reversible contraceptive; the question specifies LARC and continuous COCP requires daily adherence (Source: FSRH CEU Combined Hormonal Contraception).

explanation.summary: LARC selection is a common exam scenario testing whether a candidate can match the device profile to the patient's dual needs. The 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD is the only LARC formally licensed in Australia for heavy menstrual bleeding, reduces menstrual blood loss substantially by three months, and returns fertility promptly on removal. The implant, DMPA, and copper IUD all fail either the menorrhagia or the fertility timing constraint. In 2024 the licensed duration of the 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD was extended to eight years for contraception in Australia.
key_points: 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD treats menorrhagia and provides contraception.
DMPA can delay return of fertility for up to 12 months.
Copper IUD typically increases menstrual blood loss.
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD is licensed in Australia up to eight years for contraception (2024 update) and is first line for heavy menstrual bleeding needing contraception.

subtopic_detail: HRT route selection with VTE risk
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 52 year old woman with disabling vasomotor symptoms and moderate mood change since her periods stopped 14 months ago. Non hormonal strategies have failed and she wants to try menopausal hormone therapy.

Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2. She has a strong family history of venous thromboembolism, with her mother and sister both diagnosed with an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis in their forties. She has never had a clot herself and thrombophilia screening was declined by her haematologist as it would not change clinical management. She has an intact uterus.

Her blood pressure is 128/78, she has never smoked, and her mammogram three months ago was reported as normal.

data_table.Symptoms: Severe vasomotor symptoms and mood change; 14 months amenorrhoea
data_table.Risk factors: BMI 33 kg/m2; strong family history unprovoked VTE
data_table.Screening: Normal mammogram three months ago; BP 128/78; never smoked

lead_in: Which combined hormone therapy regimen best balances symptom relief against her risk profile?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogens with medroxyprogesterone acetate in a continuous regimen
options.rationale: Oral oestrogen roughly doubles baseline VTE risk and this combination showed the strongest breast cancer signal in the Women's Health Initiative; both matter given her VTE family history and raised BMI (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Oral oestradiol valerate with norethisterone taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Any oral oestrogen carries increased VTE risk compared with transdermal; norethisterone also has more adverse metabolic effects than micronised progesterone (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch alone without any progestogen because she is amenorrhoeic
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with an intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and increases endometrial cancer risk; progestogen protection is mandatory regardless of bleeding pattern (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch with oral micronised progesterone taken at bedtime each evening
options.rationale: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first pass hepatic effect and is not associated with increased VTE risk, and micronised progesterone has the lowest breast cancer signal among progestogens; this combination best fits raised BMI and VTE family history (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as a single tablet regimen with no separate progestogen
options.rationale: Tibolone is an option for vasomotor symptoms but has increased stroke risk in older women and increased breast cancer risk in prior breast cancer; it is not first line here given her risk profile (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

explanation.summary: The MHT route decision is the highest yield menopause exam point in Australia. Oral oestrogens raise VTE risk approximately two fold and stroke risk about 30 percent; transdermal oestradiol does not appear to raise VTE risk at standard doses and is preferred whenever thrombotic risk is elevated (raised BMI, personal or family history VTE, migraine with aura, older age). The progestogen choice matters too: micronised progesterone has the smallest breast cancer signal in observational data (E3N cohort), while synthetic progestogens including MPA and norethisterone carry a higher signal.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol avoids the VTE and stroke excess seen with oral oestrogen.
Micronised progesterone has the lowest breast cancer signal.
Progestogen is mandatory for women with an intact uterus.
explanation.pearls: Prefer transdermal oestradiol plus micronised progesterone when BMI is over 30 or there is family history of VTE - the risk profile matches these red flags precisely.

stem:
You are the GP consulting a 54 year old woman about menopausal hormone therapy for hot flushes affecting her sleep. She is 18 months into amenorrhoea and non hormonal measures have not helped enough.

She was diagnosed with oestrogen receptor positive invasive ductal breast carcinoma three years ago. She completed lumpectomy, adjuvant radiotherapy, and is on year three of five of adjuvant tamoxifen. She has no history of VTE, cardiovascular disease, or liver disease.

Her blood pressure is 122/76 and mammograms have been clear post treatment. She asks specifically whether menopausal hormone therapy would be safe for her.

data_table.Oncology history: ER positive invasive ductal breast carcinoma three years ago; on adjuvant tamoxifen
data_table.Symptoms: Vasomotor symptoms disrupting sleep; 18 months amenorrhoea
data_table.Cardiovascular: BP 122/76; no VTE or cardiovascular disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding menopausal hormone therapy?

options.text: Offer transdermal oestradiol only, as the transdermal route avoids the breast cancer risk of oral oestrogen
options.rationale: The transdermal route reduces VTE and stroke risk but does not remove the breast cancer risk; any systemic oestrogen is contraindicated in prior hormone dependent breast cancer (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Offer tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as it avoids the standard oestrogen exposure in menopausal hormone therapy
options.rationale: Tibolone increased recurrence in the LIBERATE trial of women with prior breast cancer and is contraindicated in this setting (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Offer combined transdermal oestrogen and micronised progesterone as the safest recognised regimen
options.rationale: Any systemic oestrogen regimen is contraindicated after hormone dependent breast cancer regardless of the progestogen chosen (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Decline systemic menopausal hormone therapy and offer non hormonal pharmacological options
options.rationale: A history of hormone dependent breast cancer is an absolute contraindication to systemic MHT; SSRIs, SNRIs, gabapentin, or oxybutynin are recommended non hormonal alternatives (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

options.text: Continue tamoxifen alone as it will treat both her cancer and her vasomotor symptoms adequately
options.rationale: Tamoxifen is a partial agonist that often worsens vasomotor symptoms rather than relieving them (Source: RANZCOG Menopause hormone therapy).

explanation.summary: Hormone dependent breast cancer is one of a short list of absolute contraindications to systemic menopausal hormone therapy along with undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active hormone dependent malignancy, acute liver disease, and personal history of unprovoked VTE (relative in the last case for transdermal use with anticoagulation). Non hormonal pharmacological options include venlafaxine, escitalopram, gabapentin, clonidine, and oxybutynin; local vaginal oestrogen in low dose may be considered case by case with oncology input for genitourinary symptoms only.
key_points: Prior hormone dependent breast cancer contraindicates systemic MHT.
Non hormonal alternatives include SSRIs, SNRIs, gabapentin, oxybutynin.
Tamoxifen commonly worsens vasomotor symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Venlafaxine 37.5-75 mg daily is a first line non hormonal option for vasomotor symptoms in women who cannot use MHT.

subtopic_detail: Admission criteria and first line antiemetic
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 26 year old primigravid woman at 9 weeks by dating scan. She reports vomiting more than eight times per day for the past week and cannot keep down even sips of water since yesterday morning. She has lost 4.5 kg from her booking weight of 62 kg.

On examination her lips and mucous membranes are dry and skin turgor is reduced. Her pregnancy is a singleton and she has no history of thyroid disease or previous hyperemesis. She takes no regular medications.

Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6. Urine dipstick shows ketones 3+ and specific gravity 1.030. Serum sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), and thyroid function tests are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 96/58, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; 4.5 kg weight loss
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+; sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home on oral doxylamine and pyridoxine with a review in 48 hours for symptom reassessment
options.rationale: Oral antiemetics alone are insufficient when the patient cannot tolerate fluids and has electrolyte derangement and ketosis; admission for IV therapy is required (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Prescribe oral ondansetron and arrange outpatient IV fluids in the day therapy unit tomorrow
options.rationale: Delaying rehydration is unsafe with her degree of dehydration and hypokalaemia; inpatient IV therapy is indicated now (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Arrange urgent ultrasound to exclude molar pregnancy before initiating any parenteral therapy today
options.rationale: Ultrasound is part of the workup to exclude molar and multiple pregnancy but does not delay resuscitation; the priority is IV rehydration and thiamine (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Commence prednisolone 40 mg orally daily as a corticosteroid rescue with tapering over two weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after failure of standard antiemetics and IV therapy; they are not first line and carry cleft palate concerns before 10 weeks (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Admit for intravenous rehydration, potassium replacement, thiamine, and regular antiemetics
options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with ketonuria, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, tachycardia, and inability to tolerate oral fluids meets admission criteria; IV fluids with potassium and thiamine reduce Wernicke risk (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by intractable nausea and vomiting in pregnancy with weight loss (typically over 5 percent), dehydration, ketosis, and electrolyte disturbance. Admission is triggered by inability to tolerate oral fluids, ketonuria, weight loss over 5 percent, or electrolyte derangement. Management is IV isotonic fluids with potassium replacement, thiamine 100 mg to reduce Wernicke risk, and regular antiemetics: doxylamine plus pyridoxine, metoclopramide, and prochlorperazine are first line; ondansetron is second line with the small but real 2018 CDC signal of cleft palate before 10 weeks discussed with the patient.
key_points: Admit for IV fluids when oral fluids fail plus ketonuria or electrolyte derangement.
Give thiamine 100 mg to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
First line antiemetics: doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine.
explanation.pearls: Give IV thiamine BEFORE any glucose containing fluid in severe hyperemesis - carbohydrate load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old G2P1 at 8+3 weeks with persistent vomiting despite regular doxylamine plus pyridoxine and metoclopramide. She lost 5 kg from her booking weight and has ongoing ketonuria after two litres of intravenous crystalloid.

Her PUQE score is 14. She is otherwise well with no thyroid dysfunction, no molar features on ultrasound, and a singleton intrauterine pregnancy. She takes no other regular medications and has no drug allergies.

She asks specifically whether ondansetron is safe in her current situation. Vital signs are within normal limits after resuscitation.

data_table.Response: Ongoing vomiting despite doxylamine-pyridoxine plus metoclopramide
data_table.Gestation: 8+3 weeks by dating scan; singleton intrauterine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding ondansetron?

options.text: Withhold ondansetron until after 10 weeks and continue current first line therapy in the interim
options.rationale: Delaying second line therapy in refractory hyperemesis with persistent ketonuria is not supported; the risk balance favours use with informed consent (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Offer ondansetron after discussing the small orofacial cleft signal in first trimester exposure
options.rationale: Second line ondansetron is appropriate when first line antiemetics have failed and dehydration persists; a modest first trimester association with orofacial clefts (approximately 3 extra cases per 10,000 exposures) is discussed to allow informed consent (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Advise ondansetron is absolutely contraindicated in the first trimester due to cardiac malformation risk
options.rationale: Ondansetron is not absolutely contraindicated; cardiac malformation signals have not been consistently replicated (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Advise ondansetron is completely safe and there is no signal at all for any first trimester teratogenicity
options.rationale: This overstates safety; there is a small but consistent orofacial cleft signal that must be disclosed for informed consent (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

options.text: Switch to droperidol as first choice given the known QTc prolongation risk with ondansetron in early pregnancy
options.rationale: Droperidol is a corticosteroid sparing option in refractory hyperemesis but is generally third line; both drugs carry QTc prolongation potential (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

explanation.summary: The 2018 US CDC linked first trimester ondansetron to a small increase in orofacial clefts (absolute increase around 3 per 10,000 births). Cardiac malformation signals from earlier Scandinavian data have not consistently replicated. Australian guidance is that ondansetron is second line after doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, and prochlorperazine, but its use is justified when first line drugs fail because the maternal risks of untreated hyperemesis (Wernicke, weight loss, VTE, mental health decline) outweigh the small teratogenic signal - provided informed consent is documented.
key_points: Ondansetron is second line for hyperemesis in Australia.
Small first trimester orofacial cleft signal; disclose for informed consent.
Continue first line agents in combination where possible.
explanation.pearls: The absolute cleft risk with first trimester ondansetron is approximately 14 vs 11 per 10,000 - small but real, and disclosed as part of shared decision making.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 28 year old G1 at 29+4 weeks with a sudden gush of clear fluid one hour ago followed by ongoing leakage. Speculum examination shows pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix and a closed cervix. There are no contractions.

Booking bloods including group and screen and GBS status from 26 weeks were unremarkable, with GBS not detected on rectovaginal swab. She has no fever, abdominal tenderness, or offensive discharge.

Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, foetal heart rate 145 with reactive CTG. Foetal ultrasound shows appropriate growth and no anomalies. She has received no corticosteroids in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Speculum: Clear liquor pool in posterior fornix; cervix closed
data_table.Investigations: GBS not detected at 26 weeks; no infection markers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management set?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly, magnesium sulfate loading and maintenance infusion, and immediate induction of labour
options.rationale: PPROM at 29 weeks without infection, abruption, or non reassuring CTG is managed expectantly rather than by immediate delivery; magnesium is only started when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours (Source: RANZCOG PPROM).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin plus clavulanate, corticosteroids, and expectant management on the antenatal ward
options.rationale: Co amoxiclav is avoided in PPROM because of the ORACLE I signal of increased necrotising enterocolitis; erythromycin is the antibiotic of choice (Source: RANZCOG PPROM).

options.text: Discharge home with twice weekly outpatient CTG and weekly ultrasound surveillance after 24 hours observation
options.rationale: Inpatient management is standard for PPROM before 34 weeks because of the risk of chorioamnionitis, cord prolapse, and rapid progression to preterm labour (Source: RANZCOG PPROM).

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly, oral erythromycin 250 mg six hourly, and admit for expectant management
options.rationale: Confirmed PPROM before 34 weeks requires antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity and ten days of erythromycin (Kenyon ORACLE) to prolong latency and reduce neonatal morbidity; magnesium neuroprotection is added if delivery is anticipated within 24 hours (Source: RANZCOG Term prelabour rupture of membranes and PPROM guidance).

options.text: Tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours plus corticosteroids to buy time for lung maturity to develop fully
options.rationale: Tocolysis in PPROM is controversial and generally not recommended because contractions are absent and expectant management aims to prolong pregnancy without masking infection or abruption (Source: RANZCOG PPROM).

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes before 34 weeks needs three parallel interventions: antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity (betamethasone or dexamethasone), a ten day course of erythromycin to prolong latency, and admission for surveillance for chorioamnionitis. Magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection is added under 30 weeks (RANZCOG) when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours. Co amoxiclav is specifically avoided due to the ORACLE I necrotising enterocolitis signal.
key_points: Corticosteroids plus erythromycin plus inpatient surveillance for PPROM before 34 weeks.
Magnesium neuroprotection when delivery within 24 hours and gestation under 30 weeks (RANZCOG).
Avoid co amoxiclav in PPROM (ORACLE I NEC signal).
explanation.pearls: Erythromycin for ten days is the ORACLE II regimen; co amoxiclav is contraindicated in PPROM because of the neonatal necrotising enterocolitis signal in ORACLE I.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 32 year old G2P1 at 39+2 weeks presenting six hours after a large gush of clear fluid at home. She has had two mild irregular tightenings since arrival but is otherwise not contracting.

Her previous baby was born vaginally at term without complications. She had a positive rectovaginal group B streptococcus screen at 36 weeks in this pregnancy. Her group and hold is on file and she is Rhesus positive.

On speculum a clear liquor pool is seen; the cervix looks 1 cm dilated. Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, foetal heart rate 140 reactive. There is no offensive discharge or abdominal tenderness.

data_table.Speculum: Clear liquor pool; cervix 1 cm dilated
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.6, FHR 140 reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer expectant management for up to 96 hours before considering induction of labour
options.rationale: Term PROM with a positive GBS swab warrants immediate induction to shorten the ROM to delivery interval and reduce vertical transmission risk (Source: RANZCOG GBS).

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin, admit for 24 hours of observation, and reassess for induction tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not deliver adequate intrapartum foetal cover; intravenous intrapartum benzylpenicillin is standard for known GBS carriers in labour (Source: RANZCOG GBS).

options.text: Perform an immediate emergency caesarean because rupture of membranes with GBS is an operative indication
options.rationale: GBS colonisation is not an indication for caesarean; vaginal delivery with intrapartum antibiotics remains standard (Source: RANZCOG GBS).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until active labour is established and reassess GBS risk at that time
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics reduces the protective effect because at least four hours of pre delivery antibiotic exposure is optimal for neonatal risk reduction (Source: RANZCOG GBS).

options.text: Commence intrapartum intravenous benzylpenicillin and induce labour with oxytocin infusion now
options.rationale: With confirmed GBS colonisation and rupture of membranes at term, immediate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and induction reduce neonatal early onset GBS disease and chorioamnionitis compared with delayed induction (Source: RANZCOG Group B streptococcus in pregnancy).

explanation.summary: At term with prelabour rupture of membranes and known GBS colonisation, both TERMPROM data and RANZCOG guidance support immediate induction rather than expectant management to reduce chorioamnionitis and neonatal early onset GBS disease. Intrapartum benzylpenicillin (or cefazolin for penicillin allergic without anaphylaxis history, or clindamycin if resistance testing shows susceptibility) is the antibiotic of choice, ideally four or more hours before delivery for full effect. Vaginal birth remains the target; GBS colonisation is not an indication for caesarean.
key_points: Term PROM with positive GBS: immediate induction, not expectant management.
IV benzylpenicillin intrapartum for at least four hours before delivery.
GBS carriage alone is not an indication for caesarean.
explanation.pearls: For known GBS carriers in labour, the target is four or more hours of IV benzylpenicillin exposure before delivery for maximum neonatal protection.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a vaginal delivery. Following delivery of the head there is turtle sign and gentle downward axial traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder. The midwife has called for help and started the clock. The mother is a 30 year old G1 with a booking BMI of 33 kg/m2 and an estimated foetal weight of 4200 g on ultrasound at 39 weeks. She had gestational diabetes managed on insulin.

An epidural is in situ and providing effective analgesia. There is no episiotomy in place. The delivery bed is a standard labour bed with head end elevation currently at 30 degrees.

One minute has passed since delivery of the head. Vital signs of the mother remain within normal limits.

data_table.Maternal history: G1; BMI 33 kg/m2; insulin treated gestational diabetes; EFW 4200 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Fundal pressure applied firmly downward over the maternal abdomen by the assistant
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Symphysiotomy performed at the bedside by the attending registrar under local anaesthesia
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is a last resort manoeuvre only when internal manoeuvres and Zavanelli have failed; it is not the first line intervention (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips onto the abdomen
options.rationale: McRoberts is the first specific manoeuvre in the HELPERR sequence because it flattens the sacrum, rotates the pubic symphysis cephalad, and resolves shoulder dystocia in approximately 40 percent of cases when combined with suprapubic pressure (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement followed by emergency caesarean section
options.rationale: Zavanelli replaces the head in the pelvis for caesarean delivery only after all other manoeuvres have failed; McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are attempted first (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Continue axial traction with progressively increasing force to release the anterior shoulder
options.rationale: Excessive or lateral traction is a leading cause of brachial plexus injury and does not resolve true shoulder dystocia; a defined manoeuvre sequence is required (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is a bony impaction of the anterior shoulder on the pubic symphysis and is an obstetric emergency. The HELPERR mnemonic is one structured approach: Help called, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), suprapubic Pressure, Enter (internal manoeuvres including Rubin II and Wood's screw), Remove posterior arm, Roll onto all fours. Fundal pressure is always contraindicated. Symphysiotomy and Zavanelli are last resort manoeuvres.
key_points: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves approximately 40 percent of cases.
Fundal pressure is contraindicated at all times.
Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last resort measures.
explanation.pearls: McRoberts hyperflexion rotates the symphysis pubis about 6 cm cephalad and flattens the sacral curve - it is the first specific manoeuvre after calling for help.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar managing a shoulder dystocia in a 34 year old G3P2. Two minutes have elapsed since head delivery. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure have been applied by two experienced midwives for 60 seconds without release of the anterior shoulder.

An episiotomy is now in place. The consultant is en route from home. The mother has an epidural providing effective perineal anaesthesia and paediatrics have been called to attend. Her previous two babies were 3800 g and 4100 g and delivered vaginally without difficulty.

Maternal vital signs remain stable. The foetus was estimated at 4300 g at 39 weeks with no known congenital anomalies. The team is preparing for the next step.

data_table.Manoeuvres so far: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure for 60 seconds
data_table.Team: Two midwives, obstetric registrar, paediatrics called; consultant en route

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Perform internal rotational manoeuvre (Rubin II or Wood's screw) via the vagina
options.rationale: After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, internal rotational manoeuvres are the next step in HELPERR before delivery of the posterior arm; rotation converts a straight anteroposterior impaction to an oblique diameter (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Perform symphysiotomy at the bedside using a scalpel with local anaesthetic infiltration
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is reserved for settings where internal manoeuvres and Zavanelli have failed and caesarean is unavailable; internal manoeuvres are attempted first (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Attempt Zavanelli cephalic replacement and transfer to theatre for caesarean delivery
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last resort when internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; it is not attempted before those steps (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Apply firm downward and lateral traction on the foetal head with McRoberts positioning
options.rationale: Lateral traction is a major cause of brachial plexus injury and Erb palsy; only axial traction is used, and only after a manoeuvre has released the shoulder (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

options.text: Apply strong fundal pressure while the midwife maintains suprapubic pressure over the abdomen
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and can cause uterine rupture (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia).

explanation.summary: The HELPERR sequence progresses if the shoulder does not release. After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the next step is Enter for internal manoeuvres (Rubin II presses on the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder; Wood's screw rotates the posterior shoulder anteriorly). If rotation fails, delivery of the posterior arm is attempted. All fours (Gaskin) is an alternative early manoeuvre in low resource settings or when the mother can be repositioned. Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last resort.
key_points: Internal rotation is the next step after failed McRoberts and suprapubic pressure.
Delivery of the posterior arm follows if rotation fails.
Lateral traction and fundal pressure are contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: Rubin II applies pressure to the back of the anterior shoulder to rotate it forward - the wrist rotates inward, adducting the shoulder into the oblique diameter.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old G1 with a known monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 20 weeks. She is asymptomatic but has come for a routine fortnightly surveillance scan.

Ultrasound today reports twin A with amniotic fluid deepest vertical pocket of 1.6 cm and a small stuck bladder, and twin B with deepest vertical pocket of 8.5 cm and a large bladder. Estimated foetal weights are on the 35th centile for twin A and the 60th centile for twin B. Umbilical artery Doppler indices are within normal limits for both twins.

Foetal cardiac views for both twins appear structurally normal. There is no cervical shortening. Maternal vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Twin A: DVP 1.6 cm; small stuck bladder; EFW 35th centile
data_table.Twin B: DVP 8.5 cm; large bladder; EFW 60th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue fortnightly ultrasound surveillance and reassess in two weeks
options.rationale: The DVP criteria for TTTS are met today (over 8 cm and under 2 cm) so continuing routine surveillance without referral would delay definitive treatment (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Deliver by emergency caesarean now because of established twin twin transfusion syndrome
options.rationale: At 20 weeks the foetuses are pre viable and delivery is not appropriate; the treatment for TTTS before 26 weeks is foetoscopic laser (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Urgent referral to a foetal medicine unit for consideration of foetoscopic laser ablation
options.rationale: Twin twin transfusion syndrome is diagnosed by the polyhydramnios oligohydramnios sequence (DVP over 8 cm and under 2 cm) in MCDA twins; laser ablation of placental anastomoses before 26 weeks improves survival in stage 2 and above disease (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Perform amnioreduction only, without foetoscopy, and continue expectant management thereafter
options.rationale: Amnioreduction alone is less effective than laser for stage 2 or higher TTTS (Eurofoetus trial) and is generally reserved when laser is unavailable (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Commence indomethacin to reduce foetal urine output and improve the amniotic fluid disparity
options.rationale: Indomethacin is not the treatment for TTTS and carries foetal renal and ductal risks; laser ablation is the definitive therapy (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Twin twin transfusion syndrome complicates about 10 to 15 percent of monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies. Diagnostic ultrasound criteria are the polyhydramnios oligohydramnios sequence: deepest vertical pocket of over 8 cm in the recipient and under 2 cm in the donor, with visualisable bladder discordance. Quintero staging (I to V) guides management. Foetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses (Solomon technique) before 26 weeks is the treatment of choice for stage II or higher, with improved dual survival compared with serial amnioreduction (Eurofoetus trial).
key_points: TTTS diagnosis: DVP over 8 cm and under 2 cm in MCDA twins.
Foetoscopic laser is first line for stage II or above before 26 weeks.
Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in MCDA pregnancies for surveillance.
explanation.pearls: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks is standard MCDA surveillance because TTTS most commonly manifests between 16 and 26 weeks.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 32 year old G1 with an uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 36 weeks. Growth on serial scans has been concordant with both twins on the 50th centile and normal Doppler indices.

Twin A is cephalic; twin B is cephalic. Cervical length has been stable and there is no history of preterm labour, hypertension, or diabetes. She has been well throughout and asks about the timing and mode of delivery.

Her vital signs are within normal limits and her booking BMI is 26 kg/m2. She has no contraindications to vaginal birth.

data_table.Presentation: Twin A cephalic; twin B cephalic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Plan delivery at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks with vaginal birth as the mode of delivery
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends delivery of uncomplicated DCDA twins between 37+0 and 37+6 weeks because stillbirth risk rises beyond that gestation, and vaginal birth is appropriate when twin A is cephalic (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Plan delivery at 38+0 to 38+6 weeks with vaginal birth as the mode of delivery
options.rationale: Delivery beyond 38 weeks in DCDA twins is associated with increased stillbirth risk compared with delivery between 37+0 and 37+6 (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Plan delivery at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks by elective caesarean section for maternal safety reasons
options.rationale: Elective caesarean at 36 weeks is not indicated when both twins are cephalic and the pregnancy is uncomplicated; vaginal birth is preferred (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Plan delivery at 34+0 to 34+6 weeks by elective caesarean section with antenatal corticosteroid cover
options.rationale: Delivery at 34 weeks is not indicated for uncomplicated DCDA twins and carries iatrogenic prematurity risk (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

options.text: Continue expectant management to 40 weeks with weekly CTG and biophysical profile monitoring
options.rationale: Expectant management to 40 weeks in DCDA twins increases perinatal mortality compared with planned delivery at 37 weeks (Source: RANZCOG Multiple pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Australian recommendations for uncomplicated twin delivery are DCDA at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks and MCDA at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks, with MCMA (rare) at 32 to 34 weeks by caesarean. Vaginal birth is appropriate when twin A is cephalic, regardless of the presentation of twin B, provided there is skilled attendance for internal manoeuvres (internal podalic version and breech extraction for a non cephalic second twin). The Twin Birth Study showed no benefit for routine caesarean when twin A is cephalic.
key_points: Deliver uncomplicated DCDA twins at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks.
Vaginal birth appropriate when twin A is cephalic.
Skilled attendance for internal manoeuvres on twin B.
explanation.pearls: MCDA uncomplicated: deliver 36+0 to 36+6; DCDA uncomplicated: 37+0 to 37+6; MCMA (rare): 32 to 34 weeks by caesarean.

stem:
You are the GP consulting a 30 year old woman who has been trying to conceive with her male partner for 15 months without success. She has regular 28 day menstrual cycles with a five day flow and mid cycle mucous change she can identify.

She has never been pregnant. She has no history of pelvic infection, prior abdominal surgery, or endometriosis. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2 and thyroid function is normal.

Her partner is 32 years old and has had one previous biological child in a former relationship. Baseline pelvic ultrasound today is normal and her rubella and varicella serology confirm immunity. She asks what she should do next to work out whether she is ovulating.

data_table.Cycle: Regular 28 day cycles; five day flow; mid cycle mucous change
data_table.Duration: 15 months of unprotected intercourse without conception
data_table.Partner: 32 year old; one prior biological child

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm ovulation?

options.text: Basal body temperature charting for three consecutive menstrual cycles at home
options.rationale: Basal body temperature has poor sensitivity and specificity for ovulation confirmation and is no longer recommended in AU fertility guidelines (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Serum anti Mullerian hormone measured on any day of the cycle to assess ovulation
options.rationale: AMH is a measure of ovarian reserve, not ovulation; it does not confirm that a given cycle is ovulatory (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Serial transvaginal ultrasound follicle tracking from day 10 to detect follicular collapse
options.rationale: Serial follicle tracking is used in assisted reproduction cycles and specific investigations, not as first line ovulation confirmation in a regularly cycling woman (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Urinary luteinising hormone testing kits used daily from cycle day 8 to detect the LH surge
options.rationale: Urinary LH kits detect the ovulation trigger but not ovulation itself; mid luteal progesterone remains the standard confirmatory test (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Serum progesterone measured seven days before the expected next menstrual period
options.rationale: A mid luteal progesterone (day 21 in a 28 day cycle, seven days before the next expected period) above 30 nmol/L confirms ovulation and is the standard initial investigation (Source: RANZCOG The investigation of infertility).

explanation.summary: Infertility workup starts after 12 months of unprotected intercourse without conception in women under 35 (six months if over 35). Baseline investigations for the woman: mid luteal progesterone for ovulation, hysterosalpingogram or HyCoSy for tubal patency, transvaginal ultrasound for pelvic anatomy, AMH for ovarian reserve, TSH, and rubella and varicella immunity. For the partner: semen analysis. Mid luteal progesterone is measured seven days before the expected next period (day 21 in a 28 day cycle, day 28 in a 35 day cycle) and confirms ovulation when above 30 nmol/L.
key_points: Mid luteal progesterone confirms ovulation (over 30 nmol/L).
Time it seven days before the expected next period, not always day 21.
AMH assesses ovarian reserve, not ovulation.
explanation.pearls: Day 21 progesterone is only correct for a 28 day cycle - the true rule is seven days before the next expected menstruation.

sources.label: Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand

stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman investigated for 14 months of unexplained subfertility. Mid luteal progesterone was 42 nmol/L on two cycles. Baseline pelvic ultrasound today shows a normal uterus, no adnexal masses, and antral follicle counts of 8 and 9.

She has no history of pelvic infection, endometriosis, or ectopic pregnancy. She is not iodine allergic. Her partner's semen analysis showed 22 million/mL concentration with 45 percent progressive motility and 5 percent normal morphology by WHO 2021 criteria.

She asks whether she needs to have a hysterosalpingogram or whether a less invasive test would work. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she is not currently taking any contraception.

data_table.Prior investigations: Mid luteal progesterone 42 nmol/L on two cycles; normal pelvic USS
data_table.History: No pelvic infection, endometriosis, or ectopic pregnancy
data_table.Partner semen analysis (WHO 2021): 22 million/mL; 45 percent progressive motility; 5 percent normal morphology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Hysterosalpingogram with fluoroscopic imaging using iodinated contrast in radiology
options.rationale: HSG is a valid tubal patency test but requires ionising radiation and iodinated contrast; HyCoSy achieves equivalent diagnostic performance without either (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Hysterosalpingo contrast sonography (HyCoSy) with saline and air microbubbles
options.rationale: HyCoSy is an office based ultrasound test with sensitivity and specificity comparable to hysterosalpingogram for tubal patency, does not use ionising radiation or iodinated contrast, and is often preferred as first line in Australia (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with methylene blue chromopertubation performed under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is more invasive and reserved for suspected endometriosis or when non invasive tests are equivocal; it is not first line for tubal patency assessment (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Serum chlamydia antibody titre alone as a non invasive proxy marker of tubal disease risk
options.rationale: Chlamydia antibody testing has poor positive predictive value for tubal disease and does not replace direct patency assessment (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with dynamic contrast to visualise the fallopian tubes
options.rationale: MRI is not first line for tubal patency assessment; HyCoSy and HSG are the standard tests (Source: RANZCOG Infertility investigation).

explanation.summary: Tubal patency assessment is a core component of fertility workup once ovulation and semen quality are confirmed. HyCoSy uses ultrasound plus a saline air foam contrast to visualise tubal spill; sensitivity and specificity are comparable with HSG (approximately 85 to 90 percent) without ionising radiation or iodinated contrast. HSG remains a valid alternative and is preferred by some units for uterine cavity assessment. Laparoscopy plus chromopertubation is reserved for cases where endometriosis is suspected or non invasive tests are inconclusive.
key_points: HyCoSy is a non radiation office based tubal patency test.
Diagnostic performance is comparable to HSG.
Laparoscopy is reserved for suspected endometriosis or equivocal results.
explanation.pearls: WHO 2021 lower reference limits for semen: concentration 16 million/mL, total motility 42 percent, progressive motility 30 percent, morphology 4 percent normal forms.

sources.label: WHO Laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen 2021

subtopic_detail: Quick start with recent progestogen exposure
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 25 year old woman who took ulipristal acetate 30 mg 20 hours ago after a burst condom. Her last menstrual period started 15 days ago and cycles are regular at 30 days. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she has no contraindications to hormonal contraception.

She wants to start ongoing hormonal contraception today at this appointment, and specifically asks whether she can begin the combined oral contraceptive pill straight away or whether she needs to wait. She has never used hormonal contraception before and has no personal or family history of VTE, migraine with aura, or breast cancer.

She is otherwise well. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Cycle position: Day 15 of a regular 30 day cycle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about starting hormonal contraception?

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill immediately today and use barrier cover for the next seven days
options.rationale: Starting progestogen within 120 hours of ulipristal reduces its ovulation delaying effect and increases the chance the emergency contraception fails (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill at the beginning of her next menstrual period with no cover needed
options.rationale: Waiting until the next menses is a valid Sunday start approach but unnecessary; the 120 hour delay followed by quick start is the standard evidence based approach (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Delay starting the combined oral contraceptive pill for five days, then quick start with seven days barrier cover
options.rationale: Progestogen containing contraception blunts the ovulation delaying effect of ulipristal; the FSRH and RACGP advise delaying any hormonal contraception for 120 hours after ulipristal, then quick start with seven days of barrier cover (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Take a second dose of ulipristal in five days to cover her cycle until the next menstrual period begins
options.rationale: Ulipristal is not an ongoing contraceptive; repeat dosing to bridge to the next period is not recommended and does not establish ongoing pregnancy protection (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

options.text: Insert an etonogestrel subdermal implant today and provide no barrier cover as the implant works within 24 hours
options.rationale: Any progestogen containing method (including implant, DMPA, or levonorgestrel IUD) started within 120 hours of ulipristal blunts its ovulation delaying effect (Source: FSRH CEU Emergency Contraception, adopted by RACGP).

explanation.summary: Ulipristal is a selective progesterone receptor modulator that delays ovulation by inhibiting LH surge. Any progestogen containing hormonal contraception started within 120 hours (five days) of ulipristal binds the progesterone receptor and blunts this effect, reducing the ovulation delay. The FSRH and RACGP therefore advise delaying starting any hormonal contraception for five days after ulipristal, followed by quick start with barrier cover until contraceptive protection is established (seven days for COCP, implant, IUD; two days for progestogen only pill). This is the reverse of levonorgestrel emergency contraception, after which hormonal methods can be quick started immediately.
key_points: Delay hormonal contraception for 120 hours after ulipristal.
Then quick start with seven days barrier cover (or two days for POP).
Levonorgestrel emergency contraception does not require this delay.
explanation.pearls: The five day delay is unique to ulipristal - levonorgestrel emergency contraception allows immediate quick start of hormonal contraception with standard barrier cover.

subtopic_detail: Refractory hyperemesis with hyponatraemia and confusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 24 year old G1 at 11 weeks admitted three days ago for hyperemesis. She has been vomiting persistently despite regular doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and ondansetron. She has now had five litres of intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride with added potassium over the last 48 hours.

Overnight her partner reports she has become confused and unsteady on her feet. On examination she has horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze and ataxia when asked to walk. There is no papilloedema, no focal weakness, and her Glasgow Coma Scale is 14.

Repeat sodium is now 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), and magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0). Blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is high relative to serum osmolality. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8.

data_table.Neurology: Horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze; ataxia; confusion; GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0); glucose 5.8 mmol/L
data_table.Fluid history: Five litres 0.9 percent NaCl with potassium over 48 hours
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/64, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous thiamine 500 mg three times daily and cautiously correct sodium under electrolyte specialist advice
options.rationale: The triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion in a hyperemetic pregnant woman is Wernicke encephalopathy; high dose IV thiamine (Pabrinex or equivalent) is urgent, and hyponatraemia correction must be cautious (under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours) to prevent osmotic demyelination (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum; eTG Neurology).

options.text: Give 100 mL of 3 percent hypertonic saline over 10 minutes to rapidly correct the sodium level
options.rationale: Rapid sodium correction in chronic hyponatraemia (over 8 mmol/L in 24 hours) risks osmotic demyelination; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia and given only under specialist guidance with careful monitoring (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Start intravenous glucose 10 percent as a bolus and infusion to correct hypoglycaemia before any thiamine
options.rationale: Her glucose is 5.8 mmol/L, so she is not hypoglycaemic; more importantly, glucose given before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in thiamine deficient patients (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent CT brain to exclude intracranial pathology before commencing any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is reasonable to consider but must not delay thiamine because Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis and the treatment window is narrow to prevent Korsakoff (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone as a corticosteroid rescue for refractory hyperemesis
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered for refractory hyperemesis but do not address the neurological emergency; thiamine and cautious sodium correction take priority (Source: RANZCOG Hyperemesis gravidarum).

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy is a preventable neurological emergency in hyperemesis gravidarum with a classical triad of ophthalmoplegia (usually horizontal nystagmus, sometimes lateral rectus palsy), ataxia, and confusion. Only 10 percent present with the full triad; treat empirically on any two features in a high risk patient. High dose IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for at least three days is standard. Concurrent hyponatraemia in prolonged hyperemesis is typically hypovolaemic and often chronic; correction must not exceed 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Never give glucose containing fluids before thiamine in a suspected thiamine deficient patient.
key_points: Wernicke triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion (only 10 percent complete).
IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for at least three days.
Hyponatraemia correction under 8 mmol/L per 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: Never give IV glucose before IV thiamine in prolonged hyperemesis - carbohydrate load precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy in the thiamine depleted brain.

stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman referred with six months of amenorrhoea, hot flushes, and vaginal dryness. She has no family history of early menopause and no personal history of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or pelvic surgery.

Investigations show follicle stimulating hormone 42 IU/L (postmenopausal above 30) on two samples six weeks apart, oestradiol under 100 pmol/L, and thyroid function normal. Karyotype and fragile X premutation screen have been sent by the referring GP.

She has not yet completed her family. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2, blood pressure is 118/74, and she has no history of VTE, migraine, or breast cancer. Bone mineral density scan is pending.

data_table.History: Six months amenorrhoea; vasomotor symptoms; vaginal dryness
data_table.Investigations: FSH 42 IU/L twice six weeks apart; oestradiol under 100 pmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial hormone therapy?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with continuous or cyclical use until the average natural menopause age
options.rationale: Premature ovarian insufficiency needs physiological oestrogen replacement to at least age 51 to protect bone and cardiovascular health; a COCP delivers this at premenopausal doses, provides contraception where fertility can transiently return, and is often preferred over standard menopausal doses (Source: RANZCOG Premature ovarian insufficiency).

options.text: Standard postmenopausal transdermal oestradiol 25 mcg patch with micronised progesterone
options.rationale: Standard postmenopausal doses underestimate premenopausal physiological oestrogen requirements; premature ovarian insufficiency needs premenopausal dose replacement, typically a higher patch dose or COCP (Source: RANZCOG POI).

options.text: No hormone replacement; symptoms will resolve spontaneously as the body adjusts to the new hormonal state
options.rationale: Untreated premature ovarian insufficiency accelerates osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease; hormone replacement to at least age 51 is standard of care (Source: RANZCOG POI).

options.text: Tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as a synthetic single tablet regimen without additional progestogen
options.rationale: Tibolone is not first line in premature ovarian insufficiency and does not provide contraception; premenopausal dose oestrogen replacement is preferred (Source: RANZCOG POI).

options.text: Referral for donor oocyte in vitro fertilisation without any hormonal replacement in the interim
options.rationale: Donor oocyte IVF may become part of her plan but delaying hormone replacement risks bone and cardiovascular harm; both can be pursued in parallel (Source: RANZCOG POI).

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is diagnosed by amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea for four months with FSH over 25 IU/L on two occasions at least four weeks apart in a woman under 40. Aetiology is idiopathic in most cases; screen for karyotype (Turner mosaicism), fragile X premutation, autoimmune polyglandular syndromes, and iatrogenic causes. Hormone replacement is recommended until at least the average natural menopause age (51 in Australia) to protect bone and cardiovascular health. Premenopausal dose replacement (COCP or higher dose HRT) is preferred over standard menopausal doses. Spontaneous ovulation and pregnancy occur in 5 to 10 percent, so contraception is discussed if pregnancy is not desired.
key_points: POI diagnosis: FSH over 25 IU/L on two occasions in a woman under 40.
Replace to at least age 51 to protect bone and cardiovascular health.
Premenopausal doses (COCP or higher HRT) preferred over standard menopausal doses.
explanation.pearls: Spontaneous ovulation occurs in 5 to 10 percent of POI cases; the COCP provides both physiological oestrogen replacement and contraception if pregnancy is not desired.
